justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the most recent observed price level, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts likely to produce a large gap. The slight upward tilt from one day to one week to one month reflects a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend momentum, while still acknowledging that over a month the cumulative expected move is relatively small in absolute terms compared to the uncertainty around it.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons in a manner roughly consistent with a diffusion process, where uncertainty scales with the square root of time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 52 points, capturing normal intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, this expands to about 92 points, reflecting the accumulation of daily moves and the possibility of a macro data release or geopolitical development shifting sentiment. At one month, the interval widens to roughly 190 points, acknowledging that over four weeks, a broader range of fundamental and technical developments can materially shift the price level. I also weighted the uncertainty bands slightly asymmetrically around the point estimate to reflect that sharp downside moves in risk assets tend to be faster and larger than gradual upside drifts.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a surprise central bank policy shift — either an unexpected rate hike or a dovish pivot — which historically has caused rapid, large repricing across asset classes. A sudden deterioration in credit markets, a major geopolitical shock such as an escalation in an ongoing conflict, or an unexpected earnings miss from a systemically important company could all trigger moves well beyond the stated bands. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release combined with a compression in volatility could drive prices through the upper bound, particularly if short positioning is elevated and forces a squeeze.

It is worth emphasizing that these intervals represent my uncertainty about probable outcomes, not hard boundaries. Fat-tailed distributions mean that even a 90% confidence interval will be breached more often than intuition suggests when measured across many forecasting instances. Black swan events — by definition rare and hard to anticipate — remain the primary reason to treat the outer edges of these ranges with humility rather than as firm limits.
